newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Cyberspace under copyright siege-Internet industry.
newsitem.headline: Cyberspace under copyright siege-Internet industry.

text.p: New copyright laws against piracy in cyberspace, being negotiated by an army of bureaucrats, will choke the system and clog public access to information, industry officials said on Thursday.
The warning from the network industry came as the world's diplomats continued talks under U.N. auspices in Geneva to thrash out a deal on global treaties to revise copyright laws for the digital era.

Network operators told a briefing the draft laws would hold them responsible for copyright infringements in the system, expose them to multi-billion-dollar liability and ultimately hit consumers of electronic information.

The operators from the Ad Hoc Copyright Coalition, a broad grouping of online service providers including AT&T, America Online and Netscape, complained that many officials negotiating the treaties did not even know what Internet was all about.

"The draft treaty creates very broad rights. Its unintended consequences could be potentially catastrophic. Certainly countries will adopt liability standards," said Peter Harter of U.S. Netscape Communications Corporation.

Barbara Dooley, head of Commercial Internet Exchange Association, said: "Not only these people don't understand the technology, but they actually have no experience of Internet at all. The ideas they're working with are not 21st century yet."

At the three-week negotiations, hundreds of officials and copyright experts from more than 120 countries will discuss three treaties on literary and artistic works, the rights of performers and producers of music and producers of databases.
It is not known how many of these government officials and diplomats have actually browsed the Net. The talks have been bogged down in procedures since they began on Monday.
The digital revolution has changed all the rules and ripped up traditional notions of distribution and copyrights. In Geneva, everyone is struggling to protect their vital interests.

Multi-billion-dollar copyright-based industries such as music and movie-making, campaigning hard for the treaties to sort out who owns what on the Internet, are trying to ensure they get their cut from works distributed electronically.

But an array of academic, consumer, scientific and technical groups as well as online service providers say the treaties will delay Internet, give broad powers to the entertainment industry and put extra burdens on the consumer.

Online service providers said that under the proposals, even innocent Web-surfing -- which by definition requires that a computer make temporary copies -- could be a violation of copyright rules liable to punishment.
With more than 500 million messages transmitted through the Internet every day by more than 120 million users, there is no way network compaines could act as the Big Brother, they said.

"Should we read everyone's mail and violate their privacy? How do we tell who the author is? These treaties are totally impossible to comply with," said Thomas Vinje, representing European online companies and network providers.

"These technologies are developing very rapidly. There is no way to predict what happens in a year's time," he added. "This is the wrong moment to be putting in place fundamental rules that will last 20-30 years."
